tldr: We developed SpectraTac, an ultra-compact optical tactile sensor that is only 4 mm thick and costs under $5 in materials. Without using any cameras, it accurately estimates 3D contact forces and contact regions simultaneously using just three small color sensors and LEDs.
hero_caption: Overview of the SpectraTac structure, sensor layout, working principle, and fabrication procedure. (a) 4 mm thick layered structure, (b) alternating arrangement of RGB LEDs and RGBC color sensors along the circumference at 60-degree intervals, (c) working principle where internal light is modulated by elastomer deformation, and (d) simple mold-based fabrication process.
overview:
To manipulate objects dexterously with robot hands, tactile sensors that can measure contact forces and contact locations at the fingertips in real time are essential. In particular, camera-based optical tactile sensors like GelSight have attracted considerable attention because they capture fine surface textures at the contact area. However, because they require a camera, lenses, and sufficient optical path length to focus an image, the sensors inevitably end up thick and bulky. This creates bottlenecks for fingertip integration and imposes heavy image-processing computation loads.

To address this, the research team adopted an inverse perspective: "Do we really need to capture images in the first place?" When light travels inside a transparent elastomer, deformation from contact changes both the optical path and color distribution. Leveraging this, they devised a mechanism to measure modulated light using just three miniature color sensors (RGBC sensors) instead of a camera. This is SpectraTac.

In their experiments, the team collected about 60,000 contact data points using a calibration setup equipped with a 6-axis force/torque sensor. They combined physically motivated feature engineering with a multi-task learning model. From just 12-dimensional coarse optical measurements, SpectraTac estimated 3D forces with high accuracy—achieving errors under 0.2 N for shear (horizontal) forces and under 0.5 N for normal force—while classifying 9 contact regions with an astounding 99.9% accuracy. They also demonstrated real-time operation for robotic force tracking and as an interactive game control interface.
contributions: Eliminated cameras and optical lenses entirely to achieve an ultra-thin optical tactile sensor (19.2 mm diameter, 4 mm height, under $5 material cost) that fits directly on fingertips.

Proposed an active sensing scheme that alternately arranges three RGB LEDs and three RGBC color sensors along the circumference to efficiently capture internal light propagation changes as low-dimensional spatio-spectral features.

Established a decoding framework that accurately and simultaneously estimates 6-axis force/torque and contact regions from 12-dimensional raw signals using physically motivated feature expansion, zero-anchor normalization, and masked multi-task learning.
Demonstrated practical utility for robotics and HMIs through hardware experiments featuring dynamic real-time 3D force tracking and contact-region-based game control.

sections.heading: Breaking Past the Limits of Camera-Based Tactile Sensors—Without Cameras
sections.summary: Tactile sensing is essential for improving robot hand manipulation, but conventional camera-based tactile sensors struggle with thickness and heavy image processing. This paper proposes a method combining active multi-color illumination and distributed color sensors to capture rich tactile information at fingertip scale without any cameras.
sections.details:
For robots to dexterously pinch objects and detect slippage like humans, fingertip tactile sensing is absolutely essential alongside vision. While various tactile sensors based on piezoresistive, capacitive, and magnetic principles have been developed, optical tactile sensors that read elastomer deformation optically have gained widespread popularity. Prominent examples include camera-based systems such as GelSight and DIGIT, which excel at capturing high-resolution contact shapes.

However, camera-based designs have clear drawbacks. Because they must maintain an optical path length (focal distance) between the lens and the elastomer surface, the sensors are unavoidably bulky. Furthermore, transmitting and processing tens to hundreds of thousands of pixels per frame severely strains communication bandwidth and computational resources.

Recently, researchers have explored camera-free optical sensing using optical fibers or photodetectors (photodiodes) to measure light attenuation. However, measuring only overall light intensity provides limited information, making it difficult to disambiguate complex 3D forces and contact locations simultaneously.

This inspired the authors' key insight: "Can wavelength (color) information dramatically increase information density, even with very few sensing elements?" By pairing RGB illumination with three miniature color sensors, SpectraTac simultaneously extracts spectral color and spatial asymmetry from a handful of channels, opening the door to fingertip sizing, low computational overhead, and ultra-low cost all at once.

captions.F1: Appearance of the fabricated SpectraTac prototype. As seen beside a coin, it is exceptionally thin at 19.2 mm in diameter and 4 mm in height, achieving a compact form factor ready to be mounted directly onto robot fingertips.

sections.heading: 4 mm Thin, Under $5: The Clever Alternating Layout of LEDs and Color Sensors
sections.summary: The sensor is cylindrical with a 19.2 mm diameter and a 4 mm height. On a PCB, three RGB LEDs and three RGBC color sensors alternate along the circumference at 60-degree intervals beneath transparent PDMS elastomer and a black light-blocking skin, capturing contact-induced scattering and reflection changes at minimal cost.
sections.details:
The hardware architecture and fabrication procedure of this sensor are remarkably simple and refined.

■ Structural Design (II-A)
The entire sensor is coin-sized, measuring 19.2 mm in diameter and just 4 mm in height. From bottom to top, it consists of three layers: a printed circuit board (PCB), a transparent PDMS (silicone rubber) layer, and an opaque black outer silicone skin. The core innovation lies in the board layout. Three RGBC sensors (miniature optical sensors capable of measuring Red, Green, Blue, and Clear channels) and three full-color RGB LEDs are arranged alternately along the circumference. Identical components are positioned symmetrically at 120-degree intervals, while adjacent LEDs and sensors are spaced 60 degrees apart. This deliberate configuration allows multi-directional capture of optical reflections and shadowing from all angles.

■ Working Principle (II-B)
The transparent PDMS layer provides compliance mimicking human skin while also acting as an optical waveguide. RGB light emitted by the LEDs travels through the PDMS via internal total reflection and scattering. When a finger or object presses into the surface and deforms the rubber, the local geometry changes, breaking total internal reflection conditions and causing light leakage and scattering. Consequently, both the intensity and the spectral RGB color balance received by the three color sensors shift distinctly depending on contact location. With four channels (R, G, B, C) per sensor across three locations, the sensor outputs a low-dimensional numerical vector of just 12 dimensions ($3 \times 4$). Without any image processing, it yields a highly concentrated representation of low-dimensional spatio-spectral contact features.

■ Fabrication Process (II-C)
To minimize production costs, the sensor is constructed using off-the-shelf components and a simple molding process. Commercial VEML3328 chips serve as the color sensors. For the transparent layer, PDMS base and curing agent are mixed at a 12:1 ratio to ensure optical clarity and elasticity, while the light-blocking skin uses Ecoflex 00-30 blended with black silicone pigment. This layer completely shields against ambient light noise. Using only standard electronic components and silicone materials, the material cost per sensor remains below USD 5.

sections.heading: Turning 12 Raw Values into 33 Physical Features: Multi-Task Learning for Force and Location
sections.summary: By computing chromaticity ratios and inter-sensor pairwise differences, the 12-dimensional raw signal is expanded to 33 dimensions and fed into a ResMLP multi-task learning model. Simultaneously performing 6-axis force/torque regression and 9-region contact classification, it achieved shear force errors below 0.2 N and 99.9% region accuracy.
sections.details:
The sensor outputs only 12 raw data values ($x_{\mathrm{raw}} \in \mathbb{R}^{12}$) across 3 sensing elements with 4 channels each. How to extract 3D forces and contact locations accurately from this compact signal is where the machine learning pipeline shines.

■ Data Collection and Calibration (III-A)
SpectraTac was mounted on a commercial reference 6-axis force/torque (F/T) sensor, and contact was applied using an indenter at diverse angles and force levels. Alongside 6-axis force and torque values ($F_x, F_y, F_z, M_x, M_y, M_z$), discrete labels (1 to 9, or -1 when unannotated) were assigned to indicate which of the 9 partitioned surface regions was pressed. Sampling at 20 Hz for roughly 50 minutes quickly generated a dataset of about 60,000 samples.

■ Physically Motivated Feature Expansion (III-B)
Rather than feeding the 12 raw values directly into a neural network, the authors expanded the features to 33 dimensions based on the underlying optical physics. This is a crucial step:
- Chromaticity Ratios: Calculating the ratio of each sensor's RGB values to its Clear channel ($\frac{R}{C}, \frac{G}{C}, \frac{B}{C}$) cleanly separates overall brightness attenuation caused by indentation depth from spectral (color) shifts (9 dimensions).
- Inter-Sensor Pairwise Differences: Calculating differences between pairs of sensors (e.g., $s_1 - s_2$) directly captures directional asymmetry, such as when lateral shear forces or moments dim the light on one side while brightening the opposite side (12 dimensions).
Adding these to the original 12 dimensions produces a 33-dimensional feature vector. Furthermore, force ground truth was standardized using "zero-anchor normalization." Unlike standard z-score normalization that subtracts the mean, this method divides only by the standard deviation without centering, ensuring the zero-load reference state stays at zero and suppressing baseline drift when unloaded.

■ Multi-Task Learning and Decoding Performance (III-C, III-D)
A multi-layer perceptron with residual connections (ResMLP) was adopted. Its shared latent representation branches into two output heads: a 6-axis force/torque regression head and a 9-class contact region classification head. The force loss employs component-weighted L1 loss to prioritize lateral forces ($F_x, F_y$).
Evaluation results on test data were remarkable:
- The coefficient of determination $R^2$ exceeded 0.91 across all six force/torque components.
- Mean absolute errors (MAEs) were extremely low: 0.161 N for shear force $F_x$, 0.164 N for $F_y$, and 0.429 N for normal force $F_z$ (torque errors were also below $0.004\,\mathrm{N\cdot m}$).
- Contact region classification accuracy reached 99.9%, with the rare misclassifications occurring strictly along boundaries of adjacent regions.

sections.heading: Real-Time Force Tracking and Gaming Demos Show Tactile Interface Potential
sections.summary: To evaluate real-time performance, continuous manual force-tracking experiments and a Snake game control demo using 9-region contact classification were conducted. The sensor demonstrated rapid response to dynamic force changes and intuitive directional input utilizing its compliant surface.
sections.details:
Beyond benchmark metrics, the research team conducted two practical demonstrations to test whether SpectraTac can operate in real-world scenarios.

■ Real-Time 3D Force Estimation (IV-A)
The sensor surface was pressed manually with a probe to evaluate its response under continuous, dynamic loading. Whether subjected to rapid repetitive tap pulses (Fig. 4b) or sustained pressing forces (Fig. 4c), the predicted 3-axis forces (blue lines) tracked the reference sensor measurements (red dashed lines) closely. Without the frame acquisition and processing latencies inherent to camera-based designs, the sensor responded with high speed, proving fully capable of real-time robotic grip force control.

■ Contact-Region-Based Human-Machine Interface (IV-B)
Another compelling demonstration used the sensor as a controller for the classic video game Snake. Among the 9 surface regions, the center was mapped to neutral (no action), while the surrounding 8 regions controlled the four cardinal directions. To prevent accidental triggers, a safety threshold sent commands only when normal force $F_z$ exceeded 1.0 N.
When a user pressed the sensor's edge with a finger, the deep learning model identified the pressed region instantly, redirecting the in-game snake in real time. Unlike rigid touchscreens or clicky physical buttons, SpectraTac retains elastomer compliance. This highlights its promise not only as a fingertip sensor for robots, but also as an intuitive human-machine interface (HMI) for wearables and soft input devices.

sections.heading: Conclusion and Outlook: Looking Past Cameras to New Horizons in Tactile Sensing
sections.summary: Combining active multi-color illumination with distributed color sensing enables a thin, low-cost tactile sensor that estimates 3D forces and contact locations accurately without cameras. Future directions include expanding spatial resolution and detecting dynamic tactile events such as slippage and vibrations.
sections.details:
SpectraTac represents an elegant optical tactile sensing design: instead of relying on a camera, it reads contact-induced optical modulations within an elastomer by fusing color spectra with spatial arrangements.

Operating purely on low-dimensional signals dramatically cuts computational overhead and transmission bandwidth, all while achieving a 4 mm profile and a material cost under $5. This paves an accessible path toward integrating rich tactile sensing into multi-fingered robot hands, prosthetics, and wearable devices.

Naturally, there is room for improvement. The authors identify future goals including enhancing spatial resolution, achieving finer decoupling between forces and torques, and improving calibration robustness against long-term elastomer aging. Additionally, because direct optical readout with photodetectors can support sub-millisecond response rates, the team aims to extend the system toward detecting dynamic tactile events—such as minute vibrations during slip onset—that remain challenging for camera-based tactile sensors.

takeaways: Even without cameras, combining active RGB illumination with distributed color sensors along the perimeter allows 3D forces and contact locations to be reconstructed accurately from spectral and spatial cues.

Rather than training on raw signals alone, incorporating physically motivated feature engineering—such as Clear-normalized chromaticity ratios and inter-sensor pairwise differences—is vital for baseline stability and estimation accuracy.
With an ultra-thin 4 mm height and a bill of materials under $5, the design is highly practical for multi-fingered robotic hands and as an easily replaceable, consumable tactile sensor module.
limitations: Contact location classification is currently limited to 9 discrete regions; unlike camera-based sensors like GelSight, it cannot directly image fine surface geometry or textures.

The long-term effects of elastomer-specific behaviors (such as PDMS hysteresis, stress relaxation, material aging, and ambient temperature shifts) on internal light propagation were not comprehensively evaluated.
The demonstrations assume single-point contacts, leaving the disambiguation of complex multi-contact touch patterns unaddressed.
